chunks: "In space there's a lot of ionizing radiation: protons and heavy ions from the sun and cosmic rays, plus trapped particles in the radiation belts.
When one of those hits silicon it deposits charge, and if it lands near a sensitive node in a memory cell it can flip the stored bit. That's a single-event upset, a soft error.
The hardware isn't damaged, but the data is wrong.
If it lands in a register, an instruction in cache, or a configuration bit, the program can crash or silently produce wrong results. There are worse effects too.
A particle can trigger latch-up, where a parasitic thyristor in the CMOS shorts the supply and can burn out the chip.
And over a mission, accumulated dose shifts transistor thresholds and raises leakage, so memory slowly degrades. To be resilient I'd stack defenses.

At the data level, ECC on all memories, like SECDED that corrects one bit and detects two per word, with a background scrubber that reads and rewrites memory so single errors don't pile up into uncorrectable double errors.
For critical logic, redundancy: triple modular redundancy with voting, or lockstep cores with comparison.
At the part level, use radiation-hardened or radiation-tolerant devices, and add latch-up protection, like current limiting and fast power cycling.

At the system level, add watchdogs, checksums on code and configuration, periodic reloading from protected non-volatile memory, and safe-mode recovery, and shielding helps a bit but can't stop high-energy particles.
Which of these I'd pick depends on the mission length, orbit and cost."
